senses.gloss:
Devakī
------------------------------------------
One of the several epithets of Śrī कृष्ण is ‘Devakīnandana,’ ‘One who gives joy to देवकी’. देवकी was his मोथेर् and Vasudeva, the ड़थेर्.
Devakī was one of the seven daughters of king Devaka of the race of Yadus. She and Vasudeva were Pṛśni and Sutapā in a previous life. They had performed severe penance and had asked the boon from विष्णु that he should be born as their son in a future इन्चर्नतिओन्.
After मर्रिअगे to Vasudeva, when the tyrant कṁस, her cousin, was taking the couple out in a chariot driven by himself, a voice from the void predicted that her eighth child would kill him. This enraged कṁस so much that he tried to kill her then and there. Her life was saved on the intervention of Vasudeva who promised to hand over all the children born of her. कṁस imprisoned the couple and killed all the six babies born to them one after another. The seventh baby was mysteriously transferred to the womb of रोहिणी, the elder wife of Vasudeva. He was बलराम, the elder brother of Śrī कृष्ण. The eighth child was Śrī कृष्ण who later on killed कṁस, to the great relief of all.
After the exit of Śrī कृष्ण from the world and the death of Vasudeva, देवकी along with रोहिणी, gave up her body in the funeral fire (in sahagamana).

Devībhāgavata
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् or Hindu mythological lore, have been classed among the secondary scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्. Yet, modern Hindu religious practices are, for the most part, dependent on them.
The great antiquity of the core content of the पुराणस्, known as Purānāsaṁhitā, is, by now, well-established. Over the centuries, it gave rise to the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas as we know them today. Its derivatives include the eighteen उपपुराणस् (minor works) also. The Devībhāgavata is one of the more well-known and fairly popular पुराणस्.
Whether the Devībhāgavata is a महापुराण or only an Upapurāṇa, has been a contentious issue. If the Vaiṣṇavas (followers of the विष्णु cult) argue that the Bhāgavata in the list of Mahāpurāṇas is the Viṣṇubhāgavata, the Śāktas (followers of the cult of शक्ति or the Divine मोथेर्) vehemently assert that it is the Devībhāgavata that is meant. Since controversies lead to unnecessary and undesirable conflicts, and obstruct the process of spiritual evolution, it is better to ignore them.
Some scholars opine that a शाक्त ब्राह्मण of वाराणसी (or काशी) might have composed it during the 11th or the 12th century.
However, the text follows the general pattern of the other पुराणस्.
King जनमेजय (son of the well-known king परीक्षित् and grandson of अर्जुन, the famous Pāṇḍava hero) incurred great sin for having massacred innumerable serpents in his सर्पयाग (Serpent-sacrifice, akin to a black-magical rite). He had performed it to avenge the death of his ड़थेर् by the bite of तक्षक, the king of reptiles.
To ward off the effects of this sin the sage व्यास taught him this Devī-bhāgavata.
As the very name indicates, the main content of the work is the story of the exploits of the देवी (Mother Divine). It is almost identical with—though in greater detail—the story as delineated in the more well-known, but much shorter, work, the Devīmāhātmya.
There are 12 skandhas or Books, the number of adhyāyas (Chapters) and ślokas (couplets or verses) being 318 and 18,457 respectively.
A brief synopsis of the contents may now be given here, to get an idea of this work:
Skandha 1 (chs. 20; śls. 1184)
Stories of शुक, हयग्रीव, मधु and कैटभ and ब्रह्मा’s prayer to the देवी find a prominent place in this book.
Skandha 2 (chs. 12; śls. 723)
Stories of व्यास, Śantanu, भीष्म and the Pāṇḍavas are delineated here.
Skandha 3 (chs. 30; śls. 1746)
Story of the king सुदर्शन of काशी who was a great devotee of the देवी and at whose request the देवी stayed back there as also details of the दुर्गापूजा, known as Śaran-navarātri-vrata, the origin of which goes back to Śrī राम’s first worship as per the advice of the sage नारद find a prominent place in this section.
Skandha 4 (chs. 25; śls. 1416)
Doctrine of कर्म, stories of नर-नारायण and of कृष्ण are the main contents of this skandha.
Skandha 5 (chs. 35; śls. 2094)
This skandha contains the entire story of the Devīmāhātmya (also known as Durgāsaptaśatī and Caṇḍī) but in greater detail. The story of महिषासुर’s birth and of his falling in love with the देवी before being obliged to fight with her and be killed, is an additional feature. The rest of the story is the same as in the other work.
(See DEVĪMĀHĀTMYA for the details of the story.)
Skandha 6 (chs. 31; śls. 1888)
Stories of वृत्रासुर, नहुष, Śunśśepha as also of नारद’s being deluded by the power of all-bewitching māyā of Lord विष्णु are the main themes dealt with here.
Skandha 7 (chs. 40; śls. 2245)
Apart from stories and legends of the princess Sukanyā and her husband, the sage च्यवन, of त्रिशङ्कु, हरिश्चन्द्र and विश्वामित्र, this skandha gives many details of the various aspects of the देवी like शाकम्भरी and गौरी. Some miscellaneous topics like योग, भक्तियोग, temples of देवी and her worship have also been dealt with.
Skandha 8 (chs. 24; śls. 834)
The special feature of this section is a detailed description of world geography, of भारतवर्ष (India), some astronomical factors as also a description of hells.
Skandha 9 (chs. 50; śls. 3617)
By far, this is the biggest of all the skandhas of this work. The well-known and popular story of सावित्री, other less known legends like that of महालक्ष्मी and Maṅgalacaṇḍī find a place here. Several mantras and procedures for meditation on some aspects of देवी like राधा, दुर्गा and मनसा are also given here.
Skandha 10 (chs. 13; śls. 508)
The story of Devīmāhātmya given in greater detail in the 5th skandha has been repeated here, though in a condensed form.
Skandha 11 (chs. 24; śls. 1239)
This skandha is devoted entirely to सदाचार and पूजा, various ritualistic items connected with the daily routine of a religious person. Rules of good conduct, personal cleanliness, details of the रुद्राक्ष beads, some vratas or religious observances and vows, the सन्ध्या ritual, special worship processes, ritual repetition of the famous Gāyatrīmantra as also the details connected with the preparation and wearing of भस्म or विभूति (sacred ash, dear to शिव) are delineated in this section.
Skandha 12 (chs. 14; śls. 963)
This small book gives some details regarding the Gāyatrīmantra and दीक्षा (initiation into spiritual life). It concludes with a description of the Ambāyajña (sacrifice conducted to please the देवी) performed by the king जनमेजय.
On the whole, one has to concede, that this purāṇa successfully propagates the cult of the देवी or the Divine मोथेर् and has given a lot of additional information useful to the spiritual aspirants.

Devasenā
(‘army of the gods’)
------------------------------------------
Devasenā and Daityasenā were the daughters of Dakṣaprajāpati and hence sisters. Once they were abducted by a demon called Keśin, but were rescued by इन्द्र. When षण्मुख or सुब्रह्मण्य (also known as कार्त्तिकेय) led the army of the gods against Padmāsura and तारकासुर and killed them, इन्द्र was so pleased that he gave देवसेना in मर्रिअगे to him. बृहस्पति is said to have performed the religious rites of the मर्रिअगे. According to this story, the well-known festival day, Skandaṣaṣṭhī or सुब्रह्मण्य षष्ठी, is this day of मर्रिअगे.
Etymologically, the word could just mean ‘the army of the gods’. Since षण्मुख led that army as its chief he was called ‘Devasenāpati’ (pati = lord, master). Since the word ‘Devasenā’ is in the feminine gender, the story that ‘she’ was a princess and he was her husband could have been invented and later interpolated into the पुराणस्.

devayajña
(‘sacrifice unto the gods’)
------------------------------------------
An awareness of one’s social respons-ibilities and earnest attempts to repay one’s debts to the concerned persons gradually evolved into the principle of ऋणत्रय (three debts) even at birth. The same was expanded in scope into an allied principle of पञ्चयज्ञस्. They apply to all human beings, especially to the gṛhasthas or होउसे-holders.
Deva-ṛṇa or the debt towards the gods like इन्द्र and वरुण has to be paid back by देवयज्ञ (also spelt as दैव-यज्ञ) or offering of oblations ceremonially into the duly consecrated fire. Being pleased by (and also sustained by) such sacrificial offerings, these gods who have control over the elemental forces like rain or the growth of crops or granting worthy progeny, fulfil our desires. By thus mutually co-operating with each other both these gods and the human beings can live happily and even prosper well.
See also PAÑCAYAJÑAS and ṚṆATRAYA.

devapūjā
(‘worship of God or a deity’)
------------------------------------------
Throughout the history of mankind, human beings have been seeking—whether they know it or not—unalloyed happiness or bliss. Freedom from suffering and attainment of eternal peace and joy, have been the universally acclaimed goals of life.
From times immemorial, a firm belief in the existence of a Supernatural Being, omniscient and omnipotent, seems to have been ingrained in the very nature of man. By somehow establishing a contact with this Being, often called ‘God’, one can get whatever one wants in life. This is the conviction resulting from this belief.
Hinduism proclaims that this God is both nirākāra and nirguṇa (without any particular form or attributes) as also sākāra and saguṇa (capable of assuming any form and attributes at will). He can also manifest himself as a personality without any particular form, but with all the blessed qualities that one can imagine. Nothing prevents him, if need be, from assuming any form that a votary devotedly hankers for seeing or even incarnate here in the human form to set right the mess we create!
An illustration can make this point more clear. Water can exist in three states: ice, liquid water and water vapour or steam. Water vapour has no particular form whereas ice has. But liquid water can assume the shape of the vessel into which it is poured. In all these three states, vastu or substance is one and the same, though nāma (nomenclature) and rūpa (form) are different. Similar is the case with God.
Though हिन्दुइस्म् concedes that the gaining of freedom from all suffering and attainment of eternal bliss, are possible by adopting any one of the four well-known yogas (paths of spiritual disciplines)—Jñānayoga, भक्तियोग, राजयोग and Karmayoga—Bhaktiyoga or the path of भक्ति (devotion to God in his sākāra saguṇa aspect) is, comparatively speaking, much easier in this age, characterised as it is, by an excessive attachment to the physical body and (consequently) to physical comforts.
Once this is acknowledged, the necessity for and the role of rituals in this path of भक्ति can easily be recognised and appreciated.
Necessity of Rituals
By the word ‘rituals,’ certain religious observances and practices performed in a systematic way as per the directions given in the scriptures are meant. पूजा (worship of God or a deity), sandhyopāsanā (meditation on God as the light of knowledge and wisdom at dawn and dusk), होम (offering of oblations unto a deity in a duly consecrated fire), उपवास (ceremonial ड़स्तिन्ग्) and jāgaraṇa (keeping vigil at night as a part of spiritual discipline)—all these are rituals.
The philosophical truths contained in the वेदस्, उपनिषद्स् and other similar scriptural works are, very often, too recondite to comprehend. Apart from an incisive intellect, purity of मिन्द् resulting from a pure sinless life is necessary to understand them. Performance of rituals is one of the easier means to achieve this purity of मिन्द्. However they should be done meticulously with a proper knowledge of the spirit behind them.
Need for Icons
A great majority of human beings are incapable of even conceiving—let alone contemplate upon—God as the Supreme Power or Intelligence without any particular name or form. This is because of the limitation imposed by the body-मिन्द् complex and the consequent identification with it. However, an icon—an image or a picture or even a symbol—can definitely help in this process of contemplation, even as a limited window in our room gives us a view of the unlimited sky as long as we are sitting in it.
If the symbolical meaning and signi-ficance of the icon is understood properly, the icon itself will become an actualised form of the ideal. Then, viewing it will be almost as good as viewing the original it represents. It is akin to remembering a person when we look at his photograph.
We may also look at it in another way. An abacus is needed (and used) to teach certain fundamental concepts of arithmetic, to little children. Similarly an icon, especially the one installed in a temple, along with the associated ideas, can help us to conceive of and contemplate on God.
Icons or concrete symbols have played a prominent part in all religions.
Image Worship
Worship of images, both at home and in temples, as well as in public places of worship is widespread and popular in हिन्दुइस्म्. There is a mistaken notion that this is pure and simple idolatry. When in idolatry, the physical symbol itself is revered as God, in इमगे wओर्स्हिप्, the reverence is offered to God in and through the image.
Preparation of images of deities, worship to the deities through them, either in one’s own personal or in family shrines or even in temples seems to be an ancient custom. Reference to images is found even in the वेदस् (vide Ṛgveda 4.24.10). Worship of deities through images is explicitly referred to in the Rāmāyaṇa (Ayodhyā-kāṇḍa 20.14, 15) and Mahābhārata (Ādiparva 70.49; Anuśāsanaparva 10.20, 21).
Often, the images are replaced by symbolical objects such as śivaliṅgas, śālagrāmas and yantras, and worshipped.
External and Internal Worship
Worship of God can be either internal or external. Internal worship called ‘mānasapūjā’ is actually meditation which may be a simple process of contemplation on the form of the deity or may involve a regular ritualistic worship with all the ingredients, but all done mentally.
External worship is the worship of the deity in an image or a symbol with all the necessary articles needed for the worship as per the religious works.
When the external worship is performed properly in the right spirit, over a period of time, it may lead to greater and greater introversion. As a result, external, formal, worship may drop off by itself. Then, only internal worship or meditation can be continued.
The Conception of Arcāvatāra
Some schools of devotion have put forward the theory that God descends (= अवतार) into the image at the time of worship (= अर्चा) in a subtle form when invited through appropriate mantras. It is something like putting on the switch to make the electric current flow through a lamp and give light.
By the same लोगिच्, when an image fixed in a temple, is consecrated as per the prescribed procedure (in which प्राण-pratiṣṭhā or infusing with life, is an important aspect), the deity ‘lives’ in that image permanently, in a divine or subtle form.
Hence the worshipper has to be extraordinarily careful while performing the ritualistic worship to such consecrated images.
Pūjā or Worship
Now, the various steps involved in an actual पूजा or worship may be described.
Since external cleanliness and neatness are conducive to internal purity, the first thing to be done before starting पूजा is to clean the पूजा-room and the surrounding area thoroughly. Of course, it goes without saying, that the worshipper should take bath and wear washed and clean clothes for the पूजा. It may be a good custom even to keep two sets of clothes to be worn (by turns) only at the time of ritualistic worship.
After arranging all the vessels and materials needed for the पूजा properly, the worshipper should sit on the पूजा-seat (which should be used only for the purposes of पूजा) in such a way that he is facing the deity or keeping the deity to his left.
Generally, facing east or north is preferred and facing south is forbidden.
The whole rite of pūjā—for that matter, any religious or ritualistic act—should begin with आचमन or ceremonial sipping of water with certain mantras.
This should be followed by सङ्कल्प or religious resolve. Apart from the details of that particular day according to the Hindu चलेन्दर् (followed in the tradition of the worshipper’s family), the सङ्कल्प-मन्त्र also contains some other statements such as the destruction of one’s sins, acquisition of religious merit and some other particulars connected with the mode of worship.
Then come some purificatory processes like āsanaśuddhi (ritual sanctification of the seat), bhūtāpasāraṇa (driving away the evil spirits), puṣpaśuddhi (ritual cleansing of flowers, बिल्व and तुलसी leaves) and agniprākāracintā (erecting a wall of fire through imagination) and so on.
The next steps are प्राणायाम (breath control in aid of peace and concentration) as also भूतशुद्धि or creating a spiritual body in place of the physical one.
Prāṇapratiṣṭhā (filling the spiritual body with the presence of the deity), nyāsas (ritual purification of limbs) and mudrās (postures of fingers and hands) follow next.
Now, are taken up the most important parts of the worship—dhyāna (meditation on the deity in one’s heart and transferring the same into the image or symbol) and उपचारस् (modes of direct service).
These उपचारस् can be 5 or 10 or 16. Sometimes they are raised to 64 or even 108! But, normally, the first two are common for daily worship and 16 उपचारस् for special worship. The other two are done only in temples on very special occasions.
These उपचारस् are ceremonially offered with appropriate mantras to the deity invoked into the image or symbol.
The ten उपचारस् are: pādya (water for washing the feet), अर्घ्य (water for washing the hands), ācamanīya (water for rinsing the mouth), snānīya (giving a bath by pouring water over the image or the symbol with Vedic mantras), गन्ध (applying fresh sandal paste), puṣpa (offering of flowers, बिल्व and तुलसी leaves), धूप (waving of lighted incense sticks), dīpa (waving of a lighted lamp), naivedya (giving ड़ोओद्-offering as also drinking water) and punarācamanīya (giving water for rinsing the mouth at the end).
At the end of the worship, puṣpāñjali (offering of a handful of flowers) is laid at the feet of the deity, indicating the conclusion of the whole ritual.
Where the पूजा is done to the deity in a temporarily invoked image (as in the worship of clay icons of गणपति or दुर्गा), udvāsanā or visarjana also has to be done. It is the ceremonial withdrawal of the deity from the image, back into one’s own heart, after which the image or the symbol (like a flower) can be disposed off.
The mode of worship described so far, is according to the tāntric tradition. The Vedic tradition is slightly different from this. A brief account of the same is as follows:
Dīpajvalana (lighting the lamp and praying to it as the symbol of the deity and requesting it to burn steadily till the पूजा is over), आचमन, guruvandana (obeisance to one’s own गुरु or spiritual teacher), prayer to Vighneśvara or गणपति (for the removal of obstacles to the पूजा), ghaṇṭānāda (ringing the bell with appropriate mantras to drive away the demons and welcome the gods) (Ringing the bell is necessary at other times also as during ceremonial bath to the deity and offering incense etc.), recitation of two Vedic mantras to steady the मिन्द् (Ṛgveda 10.63.3 and 4.50.6), maṇṭapadhyāna (meditation on the miniature shrine structure, generally made of wood), āsanamantra (for purification and steadiness of the seat), प्राणायाम, सङ्कल्प, ceremonial purification of the water in the कलश (water vessel) to make it fit for using in पूजा, filling up the शङ्ख (conch) with that water and inviting its presiding deities (like सूर्य, वरुण, चन्द्र and others) to reside in it in a subtle form, sprinkling that water over all the articles of पूजा to consecrate them, न्यास with the Puruṣasūkta (Ṛgveda 10.7.90), invoking the presence of the deity into the image and offering the उपचारस्.
The sixteen उपचारस् offered are: आवाहन, आसन, pādya, अर्घ्य, ācama-nīya, स्नान, vastra (cloth) as also उपवीत (sacred thread, called ‘yajñopavīta’), गन्ध, puṣpa, धूप, dīpa, naivedya, ताम्बूल (betel leaf and nut), recitation of the Mantrapuṣpa (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka—Aruṇapraśna 78 to 84), प्रदक्षिण (circumambulation) and नमस्कार (obeisance).
Some more, traditional and interesting, aspects of this worship may now be stated.
In the पञ्चायतनपूजा (pūjā to the five standard deities viz., शिव, देवी, विष्णु, गणेश and सूर्य), one’s own family deity should be kept in the centre and the other four around it in the prescribed order.
Abhiṣeka (pouring water for giving bath to the image) is to be done with gośṛṅga (horn of a cow) to the शिवलिङ्ग and with शङ्ख to विष्णु or शालग्राम.
While offering cloth in पूजा, different types of cloth are offered to different deities, which can be known from the concerned scriptural injunctions. In the routine daily पूजा even flowers can be offered in place of cloth, as a substitute.
Dhūpa is offered to the feet and dīpa before the face of the deity. In general ārati (waving of lights), the dīpa has to be waved all over the deity’s image.
Pradakṣiṇā is to be done three times in the clockwise direction, slowly, with folded hands. Then comes sāṣṭāṅga-praṇāma, done by lying down on the chest, on the floor.
At the end, tīrtha (the consecrated water of the पूजा) and prasāda (consecrated ड़ोओद् offering) should be received by all who have taken part in the पूजा or witnessed it.
Epilogue
What has been described till now, just gives an idea of the philosophy and the spirit behind the Hindu ritualistic worship.
The Hindu scriptures themselves consider these rituals as the kindergarten of religion. When understood properly and performed meticulously, they lead to inner purity and concentration. When this concentration becomes deep, the external rituals drop off by themselves. Till then, they must be performed.

Devīmāhātmya
(‘the greatness of the देवी [or the Goddess]’)
------------------------------------------
The देवी-cult is centred round the concept and the worship of God as the Divine मोथेर्. The Devīmāhātmya as also the Devībhāgavata are the two most important works of this cult.
The roots of this cult can be traced to the Ṛgveda itself. The Ambhṛṇīsūkta (10.125.1) and the Rātrīsūkta (10.127.1) are pointers to this. Some of the minor उपनिषद्स् like the Devī Upaniṣad as also the तन्त्रस् (Śāktāgamas) have expounded this cult in greater detail.
Gradually, as the paurāṇic religion became more popular, three aspects of the Devī—Sarasvatī, लक्ष्मी and Pārvatī—were projected by the scriptures for worship and meditation. However, it is पार्वती who has been almost exclusively meant by the word ‘Devī’ and the innumerable goddesses considered as her aspects.
The Devīmāhātmya is considered as a part of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (chapters 78 to 90), though it is more likely to be an independent work, grafted on to this purāṇa later. It is also known by two more names: Durgāsaptaśatī (since it contains saptaśata or 700 verses extolling the greatness of मोथेर् दुर्गा) and चण्डी (since it deals with the exploits of the fierce goddess चण्डी or Caṇḍikā).
The work has thirteen adhyāyas or chapters divided into three Caritras or major sections as follows:
Prathamacaritra: Chapter 1.
Madhyamacaritra: Chapter 2, 3, and 4.
Uttamacaritra: Chapter 5 to 13.
These three Caritras are devoted to the exposition of the greatness of the three aspects of the देवी, viz., Mahākālī, Mahā-लक्ष्मी and Mahāsarasvatī, in that order.
The first section starts with the story of a king, सुरथ by name, and the merchant समाधि, both of whom had been deprived of their wealth and possessions by their own near and dear ones. They met at the hermitage of the sage सुमेधस्, to where they had come, seeking peace. After hearing from each other about the tragedies that had struck them, they approached the sage सुमेधस्, with the question as to why they were still mentally attached to their possessions and their relatives even though the latter had deliberately wronged them.
In his long reply the sage described this blind attachment and infatuation as the direct result of the power of मोह or māyā, the spell cast by the देवी or the Divine मोथेर् on all the living beings. When their curiosity to know more was roused, the sage started describing in detail, the stories related to her.
The first story concerns the देवी as योगनिद्रा. At the end of a कल्प (cycle of च्रेअतिओन्) नारायण was in deep sleep. Using this opportunity, two demons मधु and Kaiṭabha—tried to attack and kill ब्रह्मा (the creator, seated on the navel-lotus of नारायण). ब्रह्मा prayed to योगनिद्रा (an aspect of Kālī), to come out of नारायण so that he could wake up. She obliged, appeared before him and then disappeared. नारायण then killed the demons and rescued ब्रह्मा. With this ends the Prathamacaritra or the first section.
The second section known as the Madhyamacaritra contains the story of महिषासुर, the king of the असुरस् or demons. He had usurped the kingdom of हेअवेन् and driven away all the देवस् or gods including इन्द्र. Then these gods under the leadership of ब्रह्मा came to विष्णु and शिव and recounted their tale of woe. As the two gods got angry, and a brilliant light emerged from their faces, the energies of all the others too emerged similarly out of them, merging into one huge mass of brilliant blazing light and power, which took the form of the goddess दुर्गा. As all the gods equipped her with their respective weapons, she went to महिषासुर, challenged him for fight and ultimately killed him. The heavenly region was restored to the gods. The देवी दुर्गा promised to come to the rescue of the gods whenever they called upon her for help. Thus ends the second section.
The last section called Uttamacaritra (or Tṛtīyacaritra) begins with the outrageous misdeeds of the demon brothers, Śumbha and Niśumbha, who too, like महिषासुर, had forcibly occupied the heavenly regions and driven away the gods. Remembering the promise given by the देवी, the gods prayed to her. She manifested herself as Kauśikī दुर्गा, of bewitching beauty and started roaming about the Himālayan region. She was noticed by two servants of Śumbha who informed him about her presence in ‘his kingdom,’ stressing, on her captivating beauty. When Śumbha sent messengers to her with a proposal for मर्रिअगे, she informed them about her vow, taken out of ‘ignorance,’ to marry only him who will conquer her in combat! All attempts by Śumbha’s men, including several generals of his armed forces, to capture her, dead or alive, ended in total disaster. The देवी, with her emanations like ब्रह्माणी, नारायणी, कौमारी and others, successfully killed all the demons like Caṇḍa, मुण्ड and Raktabīja. Finally, after withdrawing them into herself, she despatched both Niśumbha and Śumbha, to the world of यम, the god of death, thereby ridding the world, of a great terror.
After listening to these exploits of the देवी and learning from the sage सुमेधस् the methods of worshipping her to get her grace, सुरथ and समाधि practised severe austerities for three years.
They got her vision and obtained, through her grace, what they wanted. सुरथ got back his kingdom whereas समाधि succeeded in attaining supreme knowledge for which alone he had hankered.
The work contains four hymns which are exquisitely beautiful and are a signal contribution to the hymnal literature.
They are:
(1) ब्रह्मा’s hymn to Yoganidrā— Ch. 1, śls. 72-87. (2) Hymn by all the gods, led by इन्द्र, expressing their gratefulness after महिषासुर was killed by Durgā— Ch. 4, śls. 1-27. This hymn is known as Indrādistuti.
(3) Hymn by all the gods, on the bank of the river गङ्गा in the Himālayas— Ch. 5, śls. 8-82. This hymn is called Aparājitāstotra.
(4) Hymn by all the gods, after Śumbha and Niśumbha were killed— Ch. 17, śls. 1-35. This hymn is the famous Nārāyaṇī-stuti.
The entire Devīmāhātmya is considered as a mantra, endowed with mystical powers. That is why a ritual recitation of the same is encouraged, nay even recommended, for the fulfilment of one’s desires.
Such a ritual recitation normally consists of the following procedure:
ācamana (ceremonial sipping of water before beginning any religious rite), prāṇā-yāma (breath-control), सङ्कल्प (religious resolve stating the details of the ritual), dīpasthāpana (lighting a lamp and offering a simple worship to it, considering as a representation of the देवी), worship of the Devīmāhātmya book used for the ceremonial chanting, repetition of the śāpoddhāramantra to ward off the effects of the curses of the sages of yore, if any, and then the actual recital.
The recital should include: Kavaca-स्तोत्र, Argalāstotra, Kīlakastotra, repetition of the well-known Navārṇamantra (which has to be received from a competent गुरु in initiation), recital of Rātrisūkta, the entire text of the Devīmāhātmya, the Devīsūkta, the Rahasyatraya (Prādhānika, Vaikṛtika and Mūrti Rahasyas), śāpoddhāramantra and kṣamāprārthanā (recital of the Aparādhakṣamāpaṇastotra).
There are several modes of chanting for specific purposes like freedom from diseases, attaining wealth or position, for the birth of children and so on. These have to be learnt from teachers who are experts in the field.
Recitations called Śatacaṇḍī (ten ब्राह्मणस् reciting it for four days—once on the first day, twice on the second day, thrice on the third day and four times on the fourth day) and Sahasracaṇḍī (with one hundred ब्राह्मणस्, the procedure being similar) are forms of congregational worship and are done for the welfare of the society.
In all these rites, होम (offering of oblations into a duly consecrated fire) is also done.
The Devīmāhātmya is highly revered even now and its recitation is quite popular.

devī
(‘the shining one’)
------------------------------------------
The ‘devī’ is the feminine counterpart of ‘deva’ and hence means a goddess.
The concept as well as the worship of God as the मोथेर् of the universe—deification into a feminine form, of the Supreme Power ruling over the universe—is as old as the human civilisation. The people of Assyria and Babylonia worshipped the goddess Ishtar, as the goddess par excellence.
There is enough evidence to believe that मोथेर्-worship existed during the इन्दुस् वल्लेय् चिविलिसतिओन् (2800 B. C.).
The Ṛgveda (2.1.11; 8.10.2) refers to several female deities as the consorts of male deities or even as independent and separate goddesses such as अदिति, उषस्, पृथ्वी, रात्रि, Vāc, श्रद्धा and so on. Sacred rivers like सरस्वती, गङ्गा, यमुना, Śutudrū and Paruṣṇī were also deified as goddesses.
In course of time, many folk-goddesses of great antiquity and uncertain origin were also absorbed into the देवी-cult.
However, it is in the paurāṇic age that the notion of the मोथेर्-goddess, देवी, came to be associated with the three prominent deities (the Trimūrtis) ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and शिव, thereby giving rise to a great number of her aspects.
The three major goddesses are सरस्वती (consort of ब्रह्मा), लक्ष्मी (consort of विष्णु) and पार्वती (consort of शिव).
In the पुराणस्, while there is an attempt to depict them as three aspects of one and the same देवी, there are also legends trying to project one of them as superior to and hence the mistress of, the other two.
By and large, an overwhelming majority of the goddesses are either different facets of the goddess पार्वती (the spouse of शिव) or her attendants or her associates. In fact, even the word ‘Devī’ has been specially reserved for her.
For details, see under each title such as LAKṢMĪ, PĀRVATĪ, SARASVATĪ.

deva-ṛṇa
(‘debt to gods’)
------------------------------------------
A human being is said to be born under the load of three ṛṇas or debts.
Deva-ṛṇa or the debt to be paid to the gods is one of them. It can be repaid by the regular and proper performance of the prescribed Vedic rites.
See ṚṆATRAYA for details.

Devāpi
------------------------------------------
Devāpi was the elder brother of the king Śantanu (father of Bhiṣma and great-grandfather of the Pāṇḍavas).
He was the eldest son of the king Pratīpa of चन्द्रवṁश (the Lunar dynasty) by his queen Sunandā.
Though he succeeded his ड़थेर् to the kingdom, he was forced to abdicate by the people in favour of Śantanu, since he became afflicted with leprosy. (Incidentally, this shows the power that the people of a country exerted on the royal होउसे even in the ancient days.) देवापि then took सṁन्यास (monastic orders) and started living independently.
During Śantanu’s rule, the country faced a severe famine. Then Śantanu went to देवापि, offered his apology and requested for his blessings. Soon afterwards, there were heavy rains and people were saved from the calamity of starvation.
Devāpi is also the name of another person, a क्षत्त्रिय by birth, who attained brāhmaṇahood through तपस् or austerity.
The king of the Cedi country who fought on behalf of the Pāṇḍavas in the कुरुक्षेत्र war and was killed by कर्ण was also known as देवापि.

devarṣi
(‘sage of the divine group’)
------------------------------------------
Sages of knowledge and wisdom (ṛṣis) as also of austerity (munis, tapasvīs) have been well-known in the Hindu scriptural works.
Among the several kinds of ṛṣis mentioned there, the devarṣis are one group.
The word ‘devarṣi’ has been defined as a ‘sage who is like a god’ or as ‘one who is revered even by the gods’.
The most well-known of all the devarṣis is नारद. The others are: अत्रि, भृगु, Kutsa, वसिष्ठ, गौतम, कश्यप and अङ्गिरस्. In other lists the names of तुम्बुरु, भरत, Parvata and देवल appear. There seems to be no unanimity in the classified lists.
See also ṚṢIS.

devadāsīs
(‘servant-maids of God’)
------------------------------------------
Human beings have a strong tendency to cast their gods also in their own mould. The things we like and love to possess or enjoy here must be dear to God too and hence he should not be deprived of them! This appears to be the लोगिच् behind the devadāsī system.
Dedicating grown-up girls to the service of God in temples and places of worship seems to have been an ancient practice. It existed in Babylonia, Cyprus, Phoenicia, Greece, Mesopotamea, Syria and Arabia, as also some countries of the South-East.
When exactly this custom began in India, is difficult to say. According to some sociologists, it might have started in the 3rd century A. D., though in the image of a female dancer discovered at मोहेन्जो दारो (2500 B. C.) some archaeologists ‘see’ a devadāsī.
The custom might have existed throughout India, but much more in the South than in the North.
Those who were dedicated to the god in a temple were often married ceremonially to the image. Thereafter they were to serve that god devotedly.
The duties of a devadāsī were, in general, as follows: Keeping the temple precincts clean and neat; preparing flower garlands and other decorative materials for the deity; मुसिच् and dancing, as a part of the temple rituals and so on.
They were expected to be adepts in मुसिच् and dancing. Hence they were specially trained in this art.
A lady could become a devadāsī in several ways. Seven such ways have been mentioned in the relevant works. They are:
(1) dattā— One who has offered herself to a temple. (2) vikrītā— One who has sold herself to a temple. (3) bhṛtyā— One who has given herself to the temple for the upkeep of her family. (4) bhaktā— One who has chosen to become a devadāsī out of devotion to the Lord. (5) hṛtā— One who has been abducted and offered to a temple. (6) alaṅkārā— One who was offered to a temple by a king or his minister as per some tradition. rudragaṇikā or gopikā— One appointed for singing and dancing in a temple as a profession. In some of the edicts found in Karnataka, the service to a god in a temple has been classified into two kinds: अङ्ग-भोग and raṅgabhoga. The former consists of direct services to the image like bath, anointing with sandal paste, burning of incense and waving of lights, offering flowers and ड़ोओद् articles and so on. The latter comprises mainly मुसिच् and dancing by the देवदासीस्.
Enough provision used to be made for their maintenance by the kings or the society through grant of lands, money and materials.
They were also given a place of honour in the society.
Whatever might have bean the original intentions behind this system—noble or devotional—it soon degenerated into prostitution with a ‘divine’ sanction. It also gave rise to exploitation of the weaker sex in the name of religion.
Though several serious attempts have been made to eradicate it through punishments to the agents or reformation of the देवदासीस् themselves, the success achieved has not been commensurate with the efforts.
Remnants of the custom continue to exist even today in some parts of Karnataka (jogiti tradition in the Ellamma temple at Saundatti, Belgaum district), Goa, Maharashtra (where the देवदासीस् are called ‘bhāvins’) and Tamil Nadu.

Devayāna
(‘the path of gods’)
------------------------------------------
Birth and death have always proved to be a deep mystery for mankind. Every religion has tried to solve this in its own way. The solution हिन्दुइस्म् offers is found in the Vedic literature—the Ṛgveda, the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and some of the उपनिषद्स् like the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and the Chāndogya.
The religion of the Ṛgveda, the earliest available record of human civilisation, is not only optimistic but also dynamic. A life lived well here, in accordance with the principles of ṛta (straightforwardness), सत्य (truth) and धर्म (righteousness), will automatically give you happiness and peace in the life hereafter also. This is the main teaching of the वेदस्, the उपनिषद्स् and all the allied scriptures.
A strong belief in an uncreated, unborn eternal सोउल्, born out of their mystical experiences, naturally made the Vedic seers reflect on its sojourn after the death of this body also. What they discovered in their moments of revelation was given expression to in some of the mantras.
Generally, three destinies for the सोउल् of a dead person have been predicated in these Vedic works: going to the Brahma-लोक (or the world of ब्रह्मा) by the Arcirādimārga (the path of light, also called देवयान or उत्तरायण), from which there is no return to this mundane existence; going to the पितृलोक or चन्द्र-लोक (the world of manes) by the Dhūmādi-mārga (the path of smoke) from which there is return after exhausting the fruits of the merit acquired earlier in this world; repeated birth and death in various bodies.
The first mention of the words देवयान and पितृयान is found in the Ṛgveda where अग्नि is addressed as the knower of the path of gods (1.72.7) and the path of the manes (10.2.7). In the मन्त्र (10.18.1) मृत्यु, the god of death, is requested to clear away from the path of gods. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa also mentions these paths in several places. The Ṛgvedic verse (10.18.1) is repeated almost verbatim in the Atharvaveda (12.2.21).
It is quite likely that the देवयान and the पितृयान were the celestial paths by which the gods (like इन्द्र) and the manes used to descend to this earth to receive their sacrificial and obsequial offerings and return. Gradually, however the paths were ‘thrown open’ as it were, to deserving human beings too.
The देवयान starts with arcis or the light of the funeral pyre and ends with the ब्रह्मलोक. Various stations are mentioned in between. The enumeration of these stations is found in the following उपनिषद्स्: Bṛhadāraṇyaka (6.2.15 and 16); Chāndogya (4.15.5 and 5.10.1 to 6); Kauṣītaki-brāhmaṇa (1.3). It is mentioned in the Bhagavadgītā (8.24) also. The stations commonly mentioned are:
Arcis (light), ahaḥ (day), āpūrya-māṇapakṣa (bright fortnight), उत्तरायण (summer solstice), saṁvatsara (year), आदित्य (sun) and candramas (moon).
At this point, an ‘amānavapuruṣa’ (a being who is not a human; a divine being) will come and take the सोउल् to ब्रह्मा in ब्रह्मलोक or सत्यलोक.
Sometimes ‘candramas’ is omitted and ‘devaloka’ is substituted for ‘saṁ-vatsara’. The divine being had also been called ‘puruṣo mānasaḥ’ (‘the मिन्द्-born person’).
The terms used in these lists such as arcis (light) or ahaḥ (day) actually refer to the ātivāhikās or divine guides on the path (vide Brahmasūtras 4.3.4).
Who are those fortunate persons considered as fit enough to tread this path and go to ब्रह्मलोक, from which there is no return? The Chāndogya (5.10.1) and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (6.2.15) उपनिषद्स् declare that the knowers of the Pañcāgni-vidyā (‘the doctrine of ड़िवे ड़िरेस्’) (See PAÑCĀGNIVIDYĀ.) as also those who live in the forests, devoted to faith, austerity and truth, go by this path. The Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad too (1.2.11) mentions that those who are self-controlled, full of knowledge and wisdom, living on alms and in forests and devoted to austerity, go by the ‘Sūryadvāra’ (i.e., देवयान) and attain the Immortal Being. The Praśna Upaniṣad (1.10) also proclaims the same thing.
Those who reach the ब्रह्मलोक are supposed to live there enjoying great peace and bliss till the end of ब्रह्मा’s life, after which they—along with the Brahma-लोक and Brahmā—get merged in परब्रह्मन् or the Supreme Spirit.
This mode of मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् is called क्रममुक्ति or gradual लिबेरतिओन्.
See also PITṚYĀNA.

Devīpurāṇa
------------------------------------------
The Devīpurāṇa is an Upapurāṇa, belonging to the cult of शक्ति worship. The printed edition available now seems to be only a part of a much bigger original. It was probably composed in Bengal in the seventh century A. D.
The book deals mainly with the exploits of the देवी, especially as विन्ध्य-vāsinī. However, many other topics also have been dealt with. They are:
Various stories connected with देवी’s incarnations; her relationship with शिव and other gods; शाक्त इचोनोग्रफ्य् and शाक्त vows; some cults of शिव, विष्णु and गणपति; construction of towns and forts; different Vedic schools; the science of medicine; holy places; giving gifts; customs and usages of people and so on.
The method of the worship of the देवी mentioned here is very different from that followed in present-day Bengal.

devatās
(‘divine beings’)
------------------------------------------
Etymologically speaking, the words ‘devatā’ and ‘deva’ mean the same thing. The देवतास् are gods or deities or divine beings endowed with extraordinary or supernatural powers.
In the Vedic literature, especially in the Ṛgveda, we come across a number of देवतास्. They are usually enumerated as 33. (See DEVAS for details.) Apart from these gods, many inanimate objects like grinding stone, qualities like faith, emotions like anger, aspects of nature like dawn have been deified and described. There are quite a few female देवतास् also though they are not as prominent as the male deities.
These deities may have an anthro-pomorphic form or may not have. As an aspect of nature or a physical object they don’t. But, as the presiding deity behind them they do have.
The Vedic deities have been allotted different places in the universe. अग्नि, पृथ्वी and Somapavamāna belong to the पृथ्वी (earth). इन्द्र, वायु and Parjanya belong to अन्तरिक्ष (sky). वरुण, मित्र, सूर्य and विष्णु belong to dyuloka (heaven).
But, ultimately, all of them are different aspects of the Supreme God, ब्रह्मन्-आत्मन्.
Sometimes these देवतास् are described as being born from one another. For instance अग्नि is born from सूर्य and again, सूर्य from अग्नि. Being too remote in point of time, it is rather difficult for us to explain these anomalies. Sometimes, even the explanations of the Nirukta by यास्क do not help us much.
The paurāṇic हिन्दुइस्म् has offered a large number of देवतास्, gods and goddesses, most of whom do not seem to have existed during the Vedic period. However, the basic idea that all of them are different aspects of one and the same Supreme God (Brahman or परमात्मन्) persists.

Devī Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a small Upaniṣad of only 32 mantras, assigned to the Atharvaveda. The mantras are both in prose and in verses. The देवी or God as the Divine मोथेर् is the main theme. Verses included here seem to have been culled out from the Devīsūkta of the Ṛgveda, the Devī-māhātmya of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa as also the Durgāsūkta of the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad.
Once all the gods approached the देवी (the मोथेर् Divine) and asked her who she was. In reply she said she was ब्रह्मन् and that the whole world comprising matter and souls, the five elements, the sacred and the secular sciences, the unborn and the born or in fact, all that exists every where, is herself. It is again she that exists in the form of the Rudras, the वसुस्, and the विश्वेदेवस् (various kinds of divine beings inhabiting the worlds). It is she that is helping विष्णु, ब्रह्मा and others to sustain themselves. Due to her power and grace only, performers of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् are able to reap their benefits.
Hearing this, the gods praised her through a beautiful hymn: Obeisance to the auspicious goddess, the origin of the universe and the brilliantly shining deity. We take refuge in her, the goddess दुर्गा, सरस्वती the mistress of speech, the consort of शिव (as दक्ष’s daughter) and the power of विष्णु (Vaiṣṇavī). We bow down to her.
The Upaniṣad then goes on to give the well-known Devīmantras like the pañcadaśākṣarī (ka e ī la hrīm, ha sa ka ha la hrīm, sa ka la hrīm) and the navākṣarī (aiṁ ह्रीṁ klīṁ cāmuṇḍāyai vicce).
It concludes with a long list of the fruits one gets by the repetition of this Upaniṣad and the mantras therein.
See also DEVĪ and UPANIṢADS.

Devīsūkta
(‘hymn of the देवी or the goddess’)
------------------------------------------
Worship of God as the मोथेर् of the universe is a very ancient practice, especially in हिन्दुइस्म्. One of the oft-quoted authorities to prove this point is the Devīsūkta of the Ṛgveda (10.125.1-8).
This सूक्त or hymn is also known as the Vāgāmbhṛṇīsūkta since it was revealed to the woman ṛṣi Vāc who was the daughter of the sage Ambhṛṇa. It has eight mantras or stanzas wherein Vāc describes her mystical experiences and her identity with परमात्मन् or God.
There are quite a few instances in the scriptural works wherein the sages who had attained mystical union with God had declared that they themselves were God (vide Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10; Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.1 and 2). Similar is the case here also.
Commentators of the विष्णु cult identify her with लक्ष्मी, the eternal consort of विष्णु-नारायण.
The first verse declares that it is she (viz., Vāgāmbhṛṇī) that is moving in the form of the various Vedic deities like the eleven Rudras, the eight वसुस्, the twelve Ādityas as also the विश्वेदेवस्. It is she who is supporting and sustaining the gods मित्र, वरुण, इन्द्र, अग्नि and the Aśvinīdevatās.
Again, it is she who is sustaining the सोम juice, and the gods त्वष्टा, भग and पूषन्. It is verily she who rewards a sacrificer when he performs it.
She is the mistress of the whole world, awarding rewards to the worshippers. She is the primary deity propitiated in the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्. She exists everywhere.
It is she who is responsible for all the psycho-physical activities in the living beings.
Those who please her by proper acts of propitiation are elevated to the level of a ṛṣi (sage, a seer of mantras) or even ब्रह्मा, the creator!
It is she that strings the bow of शिव when he decides to destroy the demons of the three cities (Tripurāsuras).
She has created the svargaloka or हेअवेन्. She has also entered into all the worlds and all the beings. She it is, who is moving freely in the universe, even like the wind.
Such is the greatness of the देवी.
In spite of all the efforts of the various commentators, the purport of this hymn seems to remain rather elusive.

Devavrata
(‘One [whose] penance [is as good as that of a] god’)
------------------------------------------
‘Devavrata’ was the original name of भीष्म, the famous grandsire of the Mahābhārata. See BHĪṢMA for details.
According to the Padmapurāṇa (Pātālakhaṇḍa, 73) देवव्रत was a ब्राह्मण who was born as a bamboo stem in the Vṛndāvana where कृष्ण lived, since he had incurred the wrath of the devotee of विष्णु and had been cursed by him. When कृष्ण cut it, made a flute out of it and started playing on it, देवव्रत was liberated.
‘Devavrata’ is also the name of a vrata or religious observance mentioned in some of the पुराणस्. Worshipping महेश्वर (Śiva) on a caturdaśī day (14th day after full-मोओन् or new-मोओन्) with the star Maghā (comprising alpha, eta, gamma, zeta and two more स्तर्स्) and the planet गुरु (Jupiter) in conjunction, will bestow long life, wealth and fame. This is one vrata called ‘Devavrata’. In another type, नक्त (eating once only at night) for eight days and gifting a golden trident and discus as also two garments is the discipline prescribed. Result promised is freedom from even grave sins.

Devahūti
------------------------------------------
In imitation of the well-known Bhagavadgītā, a number of other Gītās have appeared in the later religious literature of हिन्दुइस्म्. One of them is the Kapilagītā from the Bhāgavatam (3.25-33). Here, the great sage कपिल, reputed to be an इन्चर्नतिओन् of Lord विष्णु, teaches Sāṅkhya or spiritual wisdom, to his own मोथेर् देवहूति.
Devahūti was the second of the three daughters of Svāyambhuva मनु. She was married to the sage कर्दम and gave birth to nine daughters including अरुन्धती (wife of the sage वसिष्ठ) and अनसूया (the paragon of wifely virtues and the wife of the great sage अत्रि) and a son, कपिल.
Kapila was विष्णु himself born as their son. When कर्दम left for the forest to lead a life of retirement and austerities, he advised देवहूति to approach their divine son for spiritual knowledge. Accordingly कपिल taught her Sāṅkhyaśāstra. After teaching her, कपिल too departed for the forest.
Then देवहूति performed a sacrifice on the banks of the सरस्वती रिवेर् and did severe austerities. She thus realized the Truth and gave up the body.
See also KAPILA and KARDAMA.

Devīgītā
------------------------------------------
The Bhagavadgītā of the Mahā-bhārata has become so well-known and so highly respected as a basic scripture by itself that several Gītās in imitation of the same have been composed in later times. Some of them are parts of other bigger works like the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa and the Bhāgavata (vide Rāmagītā, Kapilagītā and Bhikṣugītā) while others like the Aṣṭāvakragītā and the Avadhūtagītā are independent works. The Devīgītā belongs to the second category.
It is in the form of a dialogue in 9 chapters between the देवी पार्वती (as the teacher) and her ड़थेर् Himavān (as the disciple). She teaches the advaita doctrine as expounded by शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820). Advaitic experience can be obtained only by meditation on the Upaniṣadic texts like tat tvam asi. Such meditation becomes possible only to those who have a strong and pure मिन्द्. This, again, can be obtained only by the proper performance of one’s duties as per one’s वर्ण (caste) and आश्रम (station in life).
Other subjects dealt with are: विश्वरूप (universal form) of the देवी; aṣṭāṅga योग or the eight steps of योग as taught by पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.); other yogas viz., those of ज्ञान, कर्म and भक्ति; temples of देवी and her worship (both Vedic and tāntrik) and so on.
Obviously it is a later work of the देवी-cult.

devas
(‘the shining ones’)
------------------------------------------
Derived from the root ‘div’ (= to shine) the word ‘deva’ represents the divine beings inhabiting the heavenly regions. They are described as the sons of the sage कश्यप from his first wife अदिति. Hence they are also known as ādityas or āditeyas.
In the Vedic literature their number is often stated as 33. The break-up is: 8 वसुस्, 11 Rudras, 12 Ādityas, इन्द्र and प्रजापति. (See under each title for details.)
But again, they are all the manifestations of the one Supreme God.
In the mythological literature—Vedic and post-Vedic—the देवस् are pictured as constantly in conflict with the असुरस् (antigods or demoniac beings). The असुरस् are probably of two types: the दैत्यस् and the दानवस्. They were the sons of दिति and Danu who too were the wives of कश्यप.
Indra was the king of the देवस् and विरोचन, of असुरस्.

Devaṇṇabhaṭṭa
------------------------------------------
Hindu scriptures have been broadly divided into two groups: Śruti and स्मृति.
The वेदस् including the उपनिषद्स् are the Śruti. All other secondary works like itihāsas, पुराणस्, smṛtis of मनु and others, as also धर्मशास्त्रस्, are clubbed together under the omnibus term ‘smṛti’.
Since the वेदस् deal only with the spiritual and otherworldly matters, gradually, a vast class of a special literature dealing more explicitly with the life here and now, both at the individual and at the social level, developed. This came to be known as ‘dharmaśāstras’.
If some of the more ancient books among the dharmasāstras like the smṛtis of मनु and याज्ञवल्क्य or the धर्म-sūtras of आपस्तम्ब or बौधायन did pioneering work in the field, later writers put forth a commendable effort in preparing compilations and digests culling the relevant topics from the earlier canonical literature.
One such well-known digest is the Smṛticandrikā of Devaṇṇbhaṭṭa, who was also known by other names such as Devaṇṇa-bhaṭṭopādhyāya, Devaṇa, Devā-नन्द and Devagaṇa. He was the son of Keśava-bhaṭṭopādhyāya and might have existed in the 12th century A. D.
The Smṛticandrikā is an extensive digest and its author claims that he has only collected in one place the opinions of various authorities, adding nothing of his own. He quotes profusely from several sources and earlier authors. He refers to विज्ञानेश्वर (author of Mitākṣarā on the Yājñavalkya Smṛti) with great respect though he differs from him on several points.
The contents of the work may be briefly summarised as follows: Various सṁस्कारस् or sacraments; duties of brahmacārins (Vedic students) and gṛhasthas (house-holders); daily duties such as सन्ध्या, śrauta and smārta rites; procedure of law-courts, partnership rules; दायभाग (See DĀYABHĀGA.); details about śrāddha and so on.
Some other writers too—like Śukadevamiśra and Āpadeva—have named their works as Smṛticandrikā, but they are not so well-known.
Devaṇṇabhaṭṭa is said to have written another work, on मुसिच् and dancing, called Saṅgītamuktāvalī.

Devanāgarī
------------------------------------------
This is the script in which the Sanskrit, Hindī and Marāṭhī languages are written at present. It is also the official script of the Indian Union.
As far as the origin of the name is considered, it is sometimes conjectured that it might have come from the नागर ब्राह्मणस् of Gujarat.
According to the modern scholars of philology, this is the original script from which many Indian language scripts have been derived. This is clear in the case of Puñjābī, Beṅgālī, Assāmese and Gujarātī scripts.
The old manuscripts written in Kannaḍa, Grantha and Nandināgarī show the script as influenced by देवनागरी.
The ब्राह्मी script has been considered as the original from which even the देवनागरी has been derived. (See BRĀHMĪ for details.) It might have evolved gradually from अशोक’s (272-232 B. C.) time upto A. D. 800.
Sometimes, the script as found after A. D. 1000 in North India is called देवनागरी and that in South India as Nandināgarī.

devayātrotsava
(‘[temple] festivals of gods’)
------------------------------------------
Ever since the elaborate rituals to consecrated images in temples became an established tradition, each temple too started having its own special celebrations. Such celebrations are called ‘yātrā’ or ‘utsava’ or ‘yātrotsava’.
There are some general rules guiding such festivals, especially regarding the auspicious days on which they should be done. The following table gives an idea of the same:
All gods—, Pūrṇimā (full-मोओन् day)
Durgā—, Navamī (ninth day after full-मोओन् or new-मोओन् day)
Lakṣmī—, Pañcamī (fifth day after full-मोओन् or new-मोओन् day)
Śiva—, Aṣṭamī or Caturdaśī (eighth day after full-मोओन् or new-मोओन् day) (fourteenth day after full-मोओन् or new-मोओन् day)
Skanda (Ṣaṇmukha)—, षष्ठी (sixth day after full-मोओन् or new-मोओन् day)
Vināyaka (Gaṇapati)—, Caturthī (fourth day after full-मोओन् or new-मोओन् day)
Of course, local customs can differ and other days may be chosen for the temple festivals.

Devala
------------------------------------------
Sages—known as ṛṣis and munis—were always held in high esteem in ancient India. The fact that अर्जुन, the principal hero of the महाभारत war, mentions the name of असित-देवल (‘Devala, the dark one’) among the great sages (vide Bhagavadgītā 10.13), shows that देवल was an ancient and highly respected sage. देवल has been described in the Mahābhārata (Ādiparva 67) as the son of Pratyūṣa who was one of the eight वसुस्. (See AṢṬAVASUS.) He was a ब्रह्मर्षि (the highest status accorded to a sage in the scriptures). धौम्य, another ṛṣi, who was the chief priest of the Pāṇḍavas, was his brother.
He is said to have been present at the सर्पयाग (snake-sacrifice) conducted by the king जनमेजय (the son of परीक्षित्, grandson of the Pāṇḍava hero अर्जुन).
In the dharmaśāstra literature, mention is often made of the Dharmasūtra of देवल. He has been profusely quoted by other, later, writers. Even शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) mentions his name. The work itself, however, has not been traced till now. Even if all that is quoted from his work by other writers is collected, edited and published, it will prove to be a valuable addition to the extant धर्म-śāstra works.
